## Article

**Fast Radio Bursts** (FRBs) are intensely luminous, millisecond-duration [[radio-transients|Radio transients]] originating at extragalactic and cosmological distances. They are fundamentally characterized by anomalously high dispersion measures (DMs)—a frequency-dependent delay in the pulse arrival time—that far exceed the maximum free electron column density expected from the Milky Way's interstellar medium [Thornton et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013Sci...341...53T/abstract). The [[rapid-variability|brief temporal durations]] and staggering energy releases of FRBs imply phenomenal brightness temperatures, often exceeding $10^{36}$ K. This extreme energy density strictly mandates a [[coherent-emission|Coherent emission]] mechanism, distinguishing FRB emission from the incoherent synchrotron radiation processes typical of most galactic and active galactic nuclei sources. Initially emerging from archival pulsar data as [[serendipitous-astronomical-discoveries|Serendipitous astronomical discoveries]], FRBs have rapidly become a cornerstone of high-energy time-domain astrophysics.

The physical origin of FRB central engines is widely believed to involve highly magnetized neutron stars. This "magnetar model" was powerfully supported by the detection of a luminous, FRB-like burst from the Galactic magnetar SGR 1935+2154 [Chatterjee et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020arXiv201210377C/abstract), [Weltman et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020Natur.587...43W/abstract). However, the discovery and sub-arcsecond localization of [[repeating-fast-radio-bursts|Repeating fast radio bursts]] have introduced significant complexity to this paradigm [Chatterjee et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017Natur.541...58C/abstract). Repeaters often exhibit distinct spectro-temporal morphologies, such as wider pulse durations and downward-drifting frequency structures. Furthermore, spectropolarimetric observations reveal that some active repeaters reside in dense, dynamically evolving magneto-ionic environments and are physically associated with compact [[persistent-radio-sources|Persistent radio sources]] [Michilli et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018Natur.553..182M/abstract). Host galaxy localizations have further deepened the mystery, revealing a bewildering diversity of environments ranging from highly active, metal-poor dwarf galaxies to ancient globular clusters. This demographic diversity drives an ongoing debate regarding whether all FRBs are produced by a single progenitor class, or if multiple formation channels—such as delayed compact binary mergers or white dwarf collapses—are required to explain the broader population.

Beyond probing extreme plasma physics and magnetospheric emission mechanisms, FRBs act as unparalleled [[cosmological-beacons|cosmological tools]]. Because a burst's DM provides a direct, integrated census of the ionized material along the line of sight, the correlation between extragalactic DM and redshift (the Macquart relation) allows astronomers to map the intergalactic medium (IGM) and precisely measure the "missing" cosmic baryon fraction. Driven by the advent of high-cadence [[radio-surveys|Radio surveys]] like CHIME and ASKAP, the observed all-sky [[event-rate|Event rate]] indicates that thousands of bursts occur daily, permitting robust demographic studies. Despite this wealth of data, significant open questions remain. Researchers are currently working to resolve whether repeating and non-repeating FRBs represent a true physical dichotomy, to decipher the lack of simultaneous [[prompt-emission-phenomena|prompt multi-wavelength counterparts]], and to untangle the degenerate DM contributions of the host galaxy from the IGM. Resolving these tensions and fully realizing FRBs as tools for precision cosmology remains a primary objective for next-generation radio observatories.

## Historical Development and Discovery

The study of fast radio bursts (FRBs) originated as one of modern astrophysics' most notable [[serendipitous-astronomical-discoveries|Serendipitous astronomical discoveries]]. The field began with the retrospective identification of the "Lorimer Burst" in archival pulsar survey data, which revealed an intensely bright, [[burst-phenomena|radio flash]] with a dispersion measure far exceeding the expected Milky Way contribution [Hessels et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018arXiv180406149H/abstract). Characterized by extremely high brightness temperatures ($\sim 10^{36}$ K) and brief durations, these early [[radio-transients|Radio transients]] were widely hypothesized to be singular, cataclysmic events, such as compact object mergers, occurring at cosmological distances. Early theoretical hypotheses even briefly explored artificial origins, such as directed beams used for powering extragalactic light sails, which yielded parameters consistent with observed FRB [[radio-frequencies|frequencies]] and energetics [Lingam et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017ApJ...837L..23L/abstract), and debated local Galactic populations fueled by controversial, since-refuted claims that the dispersion measures of early bursts occurred in discrete integer multiples [Hippke et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015arXiv150305245H/abstract).

A major paradigm shift occurred with the discovery of [[repeating-fast-radio-bursts|Repeating fast radio bursts]], which fundamentally demonstrated that at least some FRB central engines survive the energetic emission process [Cordes et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019ARA&A..57..417C/abstract). The first known repeater, FRB 121102, provided the crucial breakthrough for precise localization. Using high-resolution interferometry, astronomers localized the burst to a low-metallicity, star-forming dwarf galaxy at a redshift of $z=0.193$ [Chatterjee et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017Natur.541...58C/abstract). Furthermore, FRB 121102 was found to be spatially coincident with a [[non-thermal-radio-sources|non-thermal]] [[persistent-radio-sources|Persistent radio sources]] [Marcote et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017ApJ...834L...8M/abstract). Subsequent spectropolarimetric monitoring of the bursts revealed an extreme and highly variable Faraday rotation measure ($\text{RM} \sim 10^5 \text{ rad m}^{-2}$), indicating that the source resides in a uniquely dynamic and dense magneto-ionic environment, such as a young pulsar wind nebula or the immediate vicinity of a massive black hole [Michilli et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018Natur.553..182M/abstract).

While extragalactic detections mounted, the exact physical nature of the progenitor remained theoretical until the detection of the Galactic event FRB 200428. This burst originated within the Milky Way and was temporally coincident with an [[x-ray-flares|X-ray flare]] from the known Galactic magnetar SGR 1935+2154 [Weltman et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020Natur.587...43W/abstract), [Bochenek et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021PhDT........47B/abstract). This landmark observation provided the first direct evidence that highly magnetized neutron stars are capable of producing bursts with FRB-like spectro-temporal properties and luminosities, cementing young magnetars as the leading theoretical progenitor candidate for the broader population [Chatterjee et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020arXiv201210377C/abstract). To rigorously test the young magnetar hypothesis, systematic cross-matching efforts between CHIME FRBs and historic core-collapse supernovae in the local universe have been conducted, deriving Poisson upper limits on burst rates at these locations [Liu et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250601238L/abstract).

However, as wide-field arrays expanded the sample of localized FRBs, the demographic diversity of their host environments introduced significant tension into the standard young magnetar model. Early assumptions—heavily influenced by FRB 121102—suggested that FRBs might strictly trace young, metal-poor stellar populations, similar to the environments of [[long-duration-gamma-ray-bursts|Long-duration gamma-ray bursts]] and superluminous supernovae [Metzger et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017ApJ...841...14M/abstract). This was eventually refuted by the precise localization of other repeating sources, such as FRB 180916, which was found in a nearby massive spiral galaxy and lacked a persistent radio counterpart [Marcote et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020Natur.577..190M/abstract). 

More strikingly, the localization of FRB 20200120E to a globular cluster in the nearby galaxy M81 proved that FRB progenitors can exist in exceptionally old stellar populations [Kirsten et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022Natur.602..585K/abstract). This unresolved dichotomy suggests that either magnetars can form through delayed channels—such as the accretion-induced collapse of a white dwarf or compact binary mergers—or that FRBs are produced by multiple, distinct progenitor populations that operate across vastly different environments. In contrast to other classes of [[explosive-transients|Explosive transients]]—such as long-duration gamma-ray bursts, [[fast-x-ray-transients|Fast X-ray transients]] (FXTs), and [[luminous-fast-blue-optical-transients|Luminous fast blue optical transients]] (LFBOTs), which have been causally linked to specific progenitor systems by events like EP240414a [van Dalen et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240919056V/abstract)—the diverse host environments of FRBs continue to obscure a unified origin model.

## Physical Properties and Emission Mechanisms

Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) are characterized by their extreme luminosities and [[submillisecond-timescales|millisecond to sub-millisecond durations]]. High-time-resolution observations have resolved burst temporal structures down to [[short-timescale-variability|microsecond timescales]], with pulse rise times measured as short as $15\ \mu\text{s}$ [Cho et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020ApJ...891L..38C/abstract). The causality constraint on the source size, $R \lesssim c\Delta t$, coupled with the enormous observed fluxes, implies a phenomenal brightness temperature. Approximating the solid angle of the emission region, the brightness temperature can be estimated as:
$$T_b \approx \frac{S_\nu D^2}{2 k_B \nu^2 (\Delta t)^2}$$
where $S_\nu$ is the observed flux density, $D$ is the distance to the source, and $\nu$ is the observing frequency. For typical extragalactic FRB parameters, this yields $T_b \sim 10^{36}\text{ K}$ [Katz et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251019143K/abstract). Such extreme values grossly exceed the $\sim 10^{12}\text{ K}$ Compton limit for incoherent synchrotron radiation, mandating a [[coherent-emission|Coherent emission]] mechanism to explain the [[burst-phenomena|radio flashes]] [Luan et al. (2014)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2014ApJ...785L..26L/abstract). One prominent early theory to explain these extreme energetics is the "[[giant-pulses|supergiant pulse]]" hypothesis, which posits that FRBs are composed of discrete, sub-nanosecond coherent shot pulses, drawing parallels to the extreme nanosecond shot pulses observed from the Crab pulsar [Cordes et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016MNRAS.457..232C/abstract). Note that FRB 190614, localized to a galaxy pair at $z \sim 0.6$, exhibits a dispersion measure of $959\text{ pc cm}^{-3}$, the highest among localized bursts to date .

Spectropolarimetry offers critical insights into both the emission mechanism and the immediate circum-burst environment. A defining feature of many FRBs is their high degree of linear and circular polarization. Several bursts are nearly 100% linearly polarized [Michilli et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018Natur.553..182M/abstract), while others exhibit substantial circular fractions, reaching up to 75% in sources such as FRB 20201124A [Xu et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022Natur.609..685X/abstract). The polarization angle (PA) across the pulse profile exhibits diverse behaviors. While many bursts show flat PA curves—traditionally invoked to support emission from relativistic shocks—the recent discovery of a classic, pulsar-like "S-shaped" PA swing in FRB 20221022A strongly supports a magnetospheric origin for the emission [Mckinven et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025Natur.637...43M/abstract).

Furthermore, [[repeating-fast-radio-bursts|repeating FRBs]] are often embedded in extreme, dynamic magneto-ionic environments. This is evidenced by exceptionally high and variable Faraday rotation measures (RMs). For example, the RM of the first known repeater, FRB 121102, was observed to vary from $+1.46 \times 10^5$ to $+1.33 \times 10^5\text{ rad m}^{-2}$ over a few months [Michilli et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018Natur.553..182M/abstract), [Hilmarsson et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021ApJ...908L..10H/abstract). These dramatic RM variations indicate that the sources reside in dense, highly magnetized plasmas—such as a young supernova remnant or the vicinity of a massive black hole—and are sometimes physically associated with compact [[persistent-radio-sources|Persistent radio sources]]. Dense magnetized environments are not strictly exclusive to repeaters, however; the non-repeating FRB 110523 exhibited significant Faraday rotation and scattering, indicating local magnetization and multipath scattering within a dense nebula or the central region of its host galaxy [Masui et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015Natur.528..523M/abstract).

The consensus candidate for the FRB central engine is a highly magnetized neutron star. This magnetar engine hypothesis was solidified by the detection of a luminous, FRB-like radio burst from the Galactic magnetar SGR J1935+2154 [Weltman et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020Natur.587...43W/abstract), [Bochenek et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021PhDT........47B/abstract). Alternative progenitor models include collisions between a neutron star and a white dwarf, which yield radio luminosities and temporal widths roughly consistent with statistical FRB distributions [Liu et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018Ap&SS.363..242L/abstract). Despite this breakthrough, the precise location of the coherent radio emission remains an active debate, broadly divided between "near-field" models (where emission originates within the pulsar magnetosphere) and "far-field" models (where emission arises from relativistic shocks interacting with a surrounding medium). Recent observations of diffractive scintillation in FRB 20221022A, using two-screen scattering models, constrained the lateral size of the emission region to $R \lesssim 3 \times 10^4\text{ km}$ [Nimmo et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240611053N/abstract). This tight spatial constraint, alongside the observation of S-shaped PA swings, currently tilts the theoretical evidence in favor of emission processes operating within or just beyond the neutron star magnetosphere. In addition to multi-wavelength counterparts like [[x-ray-flares|X-ray flares]], if an FRB source resides in a close binary system, the radio burst could heat the surface of a solar-like companion star, theoretically producing a detectable optical transient seconds after the FRB [Yang et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021ApJ...920...34Y/abstract). Recent contemporaneous optical observations of FRB 20230808F, starting just 3.4 seconds after the burst, set the most stringent optical fluence limits yet for a non-repeating burst [Hanmer et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025MNRAS.tmp..277H/abstract). Furthermore, multi-messenger searches recently detected a 15.6-second GeV [[energetic-transients|gamma-ray flare]] spatially coincident with the hyperactive repeater FRB 20240114A. This flare reached an isotropic [[x-ray-luminosity|luminosity]] of $10^{48}\text{ erg s}^{-1}$, suggesting the presence of a newborn power source at the site of active repeaters [Xing et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv241106996X/abstract).

## Host Galaxies and Local Environments

The sub-arcsecond localization of [[repeating-fast-radio-bursts|Repeating fast radio bursts]] and apparently one-off events has revealed that fast radio bursts (FRBs) originate in a highly diverse range of galactic environments. The first firmly localized source, FRB 121102, was found at a redshift of $z=0.193$ within a low-metallicity dwarf host galaxy [Chatterjee et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017Natur.541...58C/abstract). This source is spatially coincident with a compact [[persistent-radio-sources|Persistent radio sources]] (PRS) emitting a [[radio-continuum-emission|continuum luminosity]] of $\sim 10^{29} \text{ erg s}^{-1} \text{ Hz}^{-1}$ [Chatterjee et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017Natur.541...58C/abstract)[Law et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022ApJ...927...55L/abstract). Furthermore, FRB 121102 exhibits an extreme, dynamically evolving magneto-ionic environment, characterized by a rest-frame Faraday rotation measure (RM) of up to $+1.46 \times 10^5 \text{ rad m}^{-2}$ [Michilli et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018Natur.553..182M/abstract). Such immense RM values and the presence of PRSs—features since observed in other highly active repeaters like FRB 20190520B and FRB 20240114A [Bhusare et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025ApJ...993..234B/abstract)—strongly suggest local plasma conditions akin to young pulsar wind nebulae, expanding supernova remnants, or the vicinities of accreting massive black holes.

However, the early hypothesis that all FRBs preferentially reside in dwarf galaxies was decisively refuted by subsequent localizations. Host galaxies vary widely in stellar mass, typically spanning $10^{9}$ to $10^{10.5} M_{\odot}$, and exhibit a broad spectrum of star-formation histories and metallicities [Bhandari et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020ApJ...895L..37B/abstract). The discovery of the non-repeating FRB 20210117A in a dwarf host with little star formation, unlike the active host of FRB 121102, further demonstrates the diversity of progenitor sources in low-mass environments [Bhandari et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023ApJ...948...67B/abstract). Furthermore, recent large-scale host galaxy analyses find no clear lower bound on gas-phase metallicity, suggesting that metallicity alone does not strictly regulate FRB production [Yamasaki et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250807688Y/abstract). For instance, the repeater FRB 180916 was localized to a star-forming region in the outskirts of a massive nearby spiral galaxy at $z=0.0337$, notably lacking both a PRS and an extreme RM [Marcote et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020Natur.577..190M/abstract). To probe the gas dynamics of these environments, astronomers have successfully obtained the first radio-based spectroscopic redshift measurement for an FRB host galaxy (FRB 20230718A) using H I 21 cm emission observations with the MeerKAT telescope, revealing ongoing interactions with a nearby companion galaxy [Glowacki et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...962L..13G/abstract). The detection of the high-redshift FRB 20220610A within a compact galaxy group at $z \sim 1$ highlights that progenitors can reside in rare, interacting environments involving multiple galaxies [Gordon et al. (2023)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023arXiv231110815G/abstract).

Statistical analyses of the broader population of localized bursts indicate a median projected galactocentric offset of $\sim 4.2 \text{ kpc}$ (or $\sim 1.0$ effective radii), with the majority of sources situated within the disks of their host galaxies [Gordon et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025ApJ...993..119G/abstract). The global properties and spatial offsets of these hosts are often statistically indistinguishable from those of core-collapse supernovae and [[short-gamma-ray-bursts|Short gamma-ray bursts]] [Bhandari et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022AJ....163...69B/abstract). This alignment suggests that FRB progenitors could originate from a mix of prompt channels tied to the deaths of massive stars (like core-collapse supernovae) and delayed channels (like the compact binary mergers that produce short gamma-ray bursts).

Conversely, observations have also definitively linked some FRBs to old stellar populations. A critical paradigm shift occurred with the localization of FRB 20200120E to a globular cluster associated with the M81 galaxy, positioned just $2 \text{ pc}$ from the cluster's optical center [Kirsten et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022Natur.602..585K/abstract). Because a globular cluster lacks the young, massive stars necessary to yield prompt core-collapse supernovae, this discovery necessitates alternative, delayed formation channels for FRB progenitors. Proposed mechanisms in these environments include the accretion-induced collapse of a white dwarf or the merger of compact object binaries [Kirsten et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022Natur.602..585K/abstract). The literature currently reflects an unresolved tension regarding whether FRBs originate from a single progenitor type capable of forming in diverse environments, or if there are multiple, distinct formation channels. In contrast to other classes of [[explosive-transients|Explosive transients]]—such as long-duration gamma-ray bursts, Fast X-ray Transients (FXTs), and Luminous Fast Blue Optical Transients (LFBOTs), which have been causally linked to specific progenitor systems by events like EP240414a [van Dalen et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240919056V/abstract)—the diverse host environments of FRBs continue to obscure a unified origin model.

## The IGM and Propagation Effects

Because they are brief, coherent [[radio-transients|Radio transients]] that propagate across cosmological distances, fast radio bursts (FRBs) encode a rich record of the intervening magneto-ionic material they traverse. The propagation effects imprinted on FRB signals—primarily dispersion, scattering, and Faraday rotation—serve as powerful and direct probes of the intergalactic medium (IGM), intervening galaxy halos, and the host galaxies themselves.

### Dispersion Measure and the Cosmic Web
The hallmark feature of an FRB is its anomalously high dispersion measure (DM), which far exceeds the maximum electron column density expected from the Milky Way's interstellar medium and halo [Thornton et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013Sci...341...53T/abstract). The total observed DM is a linear combination of components from the Milky Way, the IGM, the host galaxy, and the local circumburst environment. Before extracting the IGM component, the Milky Way's contribution must be accurately subtracted; using CHIME/FRB data, observation-based constraints place upper limits on the Milky Way halo's contribution to the total dispersion measure ranging from 52 to $111\ {\rm pc\ cm}^{-3}$ for high Galactic latitude sightlines [Cook et al. (2023)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023ApJ...946...58C/abstract).

The relationship between the IGM's DM contribution and redshift $z$—often called the Macquart relation—makes FRBs a unique tool for locating the "missing baryons" in the low-redshift universe. Using localized FRBs, astronomers have constrained the cosmic baryon fraction to $f_{\rm IGM} = 0.927 \pm 0.075$, representing an $8\%$ precision measurement that is consistent with cosmic microwave background expectations [Wang et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023ApJ...944...50W/abstract). Beyond measuring the average cosmic density, FRB sightlines can isolate overdensities in the cosmic web; for instance, statistical excesses in DM have been used to identify missing baryons hiding in large-scale cosmic filaments [Mo et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250819861M/abstract). Furthermore, the scatter in the DM-$z$ relation provides one of the first direct observational constraints on baryonic feedback, successfully rejecting no-feedback cosmological models at $>3\sigma$ confidence [Reischke et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250717742R/abstract). 

Background FRBs also offer back-lit illumination of intervening circumgalactic media. Sightlines piercing the halo of the Andromeda Galaxy (M31) have provided indirect evidence for a hot galactic halo, contributing an estimated $7$ to $169\ {\rm pc\ cm}^{-3}$ to the DM [Anna-Thomas et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025ApJ...993..221A/abstract).

### Host Galaxy and Local Environment Contributions
Extracting cosmological parameters from FRBs is complicated by the degeneracy between the IGM and the host galaxy's DM contributions. The host DM varies widely depending on galaxy type, inclination, and the progenitor's specific environment. While the typical host contribution may be relatively modest ($\sim 120\ {\rm pc\ cm}^{-3}$) [Niino et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020arXiv200512891N/abstract), sightlines through edge-on spirals or dense star-forming regions can inject highly significant excess DMs ($> 200-300\ {\rm pc\ cm}^{-3}$) [Xu et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015RAA....15.1629X/abstract). Recent analyses demonstrate a tight correlation between the excess host DM and the specific star formation rate of the host galaxy, which can be utilized to better calibrate the underlying DM-$z$ relation [Li et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025ApJ...989...77L/abstract).

### Scattering and Scintillometry
FRB pulses frequently exhibit asymmetric temporal broadening due to multipath scattering in turbulent astrophysical plasmas, typically scaling with frequency as $\tau \propto \nu^{-4.4}$ [Ravi et al. (2014)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015ApJ...799L...5R/abstract). While the Milky Way halo's scattering contribution is generally constrained to be small ($\lesssim 12\ \mu{\rm s}$ at 1 GHz) [Ocker et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021ApJ...911..102O/abstract), extreme scattering can be generated locally in the host or by intervening halos. Theoretical modeling notes that supersonic turbulence and shock-compressed gas within the host galaxy's interstellar medium can naturally produce the localized density enhancements required to explain observed millisecond scattering timescales [Xu et al. (2016)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016ApJ...832..199X/abstract). For example, FRB 20221219A exhibited a massive scattering timescale of $\tau \sim 19.2$ ms at 1.4 GHz, attributed to intersection with a partially ionized cloudlet in the circumgalactic medium of an intervening galaxy [Faber et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240514182F/abstract). 

Additionally, dynamic DM variations—both positive and negative—can occur due to plasma lensing as discrete structures move across the line of sight [Yang et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017ApJ...847...22Y/abstract). Using two-screen scintillometry models to study both Milky Way and host galaxy scattering screens, the lateral emission region of some FRBs has been constrained to sizes $\lesssim 30,000$ km, providing independent support for emission processes originating within or just outside the magnetosphere of a compact object [Nimmo et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240611053N/abstract). Statistical studies of spectral modulation suggest that diffractive scintillation may be quenched by angular broadening in the intergalactic medium for high-DM bursts [Macquart et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019ApJ...872L..19M/abstract).

### Faraday Rotation and Magnetic Fields
The linear polarization of FRBs allows the measurement of the Faraday rotation measure (RM), which probes the density-weighted magnetic field along the line of sight. Notably, [[repeating-fast-radio-bursts|Repeating fast radio bursts]] associated with [[persistent-radio-sources|Persistent radio sources]] frequently reside in extreme and dynamic magneto-ionic environments. FRB 121102 famously exhibited an extraordinary RM of $\sim 1.46 \times 10^5\ {\rm rad\ m}^{-2}$, which decayed secularly while displaying erratic short-term variations on the order of $10^3\ {\rm rad\ m}^{-2}\ {\rm week}^{-1}$ [Michilli et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018Natur.553..182M/abstract), [Hilmarsson et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021ApJ...908L..10H/abstract). Another repeater, FRB 20220529, displayed an abrupt RM jump from $21\ {\rm rad\ m}^{-2}$ to nearly $2000\ {\rm rad\ m}^{-2}$ before returning to baseline within two weeks, indicative of a dense magnetized clump—possibly a coronal mass ejection from a stellar companion—crossing the line of sight [Li et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250304727L/abstract).

In the broader, non-repeating FRB population, extragalactic RMs are typically dominated by the host galaxy's interstellar medium, leading to inferred magnetic field strengths $\sim 1-2\ \mu{\rm G}$ larger than those in the Milky Way [Sherman et al. (2023)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023ApJ...957L...8S/abstract). For sightlines with minimal host depolarization, the minimal observed Faraday rotation can also be leveraged to place upper limits on the intergalactic magnetic field in the cosmic web, restricting it to $\lesssim 21$ nG [Ravi et al. (2016)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016Sci...354.1249R/abstract). More specifically, the methodology of using the ratio of an FRB's rotation measure to its dispersion measure has been developed to specifically probe the parallel component of the intergalactic magnetic field trapped within cosmic web filaments [Akahori et al. (2016)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016ApJ...824..105A/abstract).

## FRBs as Cosmological Tools

The dispersion measure ($\mathrm{DM}$) of an extragalactic fast radio burst (FRB) provides a direct, integrated census of the line-of-sight column density of free electrons. For cosmological sources, the intergalactic medium (IGM) dominates this measurement. The correlation between the IGM dispersion measure ($\mathrm{DM}_{\mathrm{IGM}}$) and redshift ($z$) is commonly known as the Macquart relation. Because of this relationship, FRBs serve as powerful, independent cosmological probes, particularly for mapping the large-scale distribution of matter and tracing the evolutionary history of the Universe. 

### The Cosmic Baryon Fraction
The Macquart relation is a robust tool for measuring the baryon fraction in the IGM ($f_{\mathrm{IGM}}$), effectively locating the "missing baryons" of the local Universe that are too diffuse to be easily observed in emission or absorption. Recent analyses using samples of well-localized FRBs have provided precise determinations of this parameter. By modeling the probability distributions of $\mathrm{DM}_{\mathrm{IGM}}$ alongside the $\mathrm{DM}$ contributions from host galaxies, researchers have measured $f_{\mathrm{IGM}} = 0.927 \pm 0.075$, achieving an $8.0\%$ precision without requiring strong assumptions about the underlying cosmological model [Wang et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023ApJ...944...50W/abstract). To further refine these measurements, the FLIMFLAM survey utilizes spectroscopic foreground mapping and Bayesian density reconstructions to improve constraints on the cosmic baryon partition and galaxy halo profiles [Lee et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022ApJ...928....9L/abstract).

The exact form of the Macquart relation and the scatter around it depend strongly on fluctuations in the cosmic electron density. Cross-correlating the sightlines of localized FRBs with foreground galaxy surveys has revealed excess $\mathrm{DM}$ contributions originating from cosmic web filaments, confirming that these structures host a substantial fraction of the Universe's baryons [Mo et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250819861M/abstract). Furthermore, numerical simulations indicate that host galaxy dispersion varies significantly between different baryonic feedback implementations, potentially allowing FRBs to distinguish between competing cosmological feedback models [Theis et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240308611T/abstract).

### The Hubble Constant
The $\mathrm{DM}$-$z$ relation offers a methodology for measuring the Hubble constant ($H_0$), providing a novel avenue to investigate the cosmological $H_0$ tension. Using localized FRBs, constraints on $H_0$ have been derived; however, current measurements remain highly sensitive to the assumed prior for the Milky Way halo's $\mathrm{DM}$ contribution. For example, setting a flat prior on the Galactic halo contribution yields $H_0 = 95.8^{+7.8}_{-9.2} \, \mathrm{km \, s^{-1} \, Mpc^{-1}}$ under a flat $\Lambda$CDM cosmology, though upper limits strictly bound $H_0 < 89.0 \, \mathrm{km \, s^{-1} \, Mpc^{-1}}$ at a $95\%$ confidence level [Wei et al. (2023)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023ApJ...955..101W/abstract). Alternatively, a "dark siren" approach—which statistically cross-matches unlocalized FRBs with large galaxy catalogs by assuming the probability of hosting an FRB is proportional to galaxy luminosity—has yielded $H_0 = 80.4^{+24.1}_{-19.4} \, \mathrm{km \, s^{-1} \, Mpc^{-1}}$ [Zhao et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022arXiv221213433Z/abstract).

### Helium Reionization
Because the $\mathrm{DM}$ integrates the electron density from the source to the observer, the distribution of DMs for high-redshift FRBs is highly sensitive to the ionization history of the Universe. Specifically, FRBs originating at $z > 3$ can probe the epoch of Helium II reionization. Simulations indicate that the detection of $\sim 100$ FRBs in the $z = 3-4$ range could constrain the redshift of He II reionization to an uncertainty of $\sigma(z) \sim 0.5$ [Lau et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021NewA...8901627L/abstract). Furthermore, the statistical $\mathrm{DM}$ distribution of $\sim 10^4$ FRBs from a fluence-limited survey could discriminate between different reionization histories at a $6\sigma$ significance level, even in the absence of precise host galaxy redshifts [Bhattacharya et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021PhRvD.103j3526B/abstract).

### Gravitational Lensing
Strongly lensed FRBs offer unprecedented precision for cosmography. The millisecond durations of FRB pulses provide a remarkably sharp signal for tracking [[burst-arrival-times|Burst arrival times]]. If an FRB is strongly lensed by an intervening galaxy or cluster, the time delays between multiple images can be measured with extreme fractional precision. This temporal resolution is theoretically sufficient to allow for real-time observations of cosmological processes, such as cosmic expansion and the transverse proper motion of the lens [Zitrin et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018ApJ...866..101Z/abstract). Future detections of strongly lensed FRBs could theoretically constrain $H_0$ to sub-percent precision with as few as 10 systems, while also providing model-independent constraints on cosmic curvature, thereby breaking intractable degeneracies between curvature and dark energy [Li et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018NatCo...9.3833L/abstract).

### Fundamental Physics
Beyond mapping matter, the propagation of FRBs across cosmological distances enables stringent tests of fundamental physics. The frequency-dependent time delays observed in localized bursts, such as the initial observations of FRB 150418, have been utilized to place strict limits on Einstein's Equivalence Principle by constraining the differential post-Newtonian parameter $\gamma$ across different radio frequencies [Tingay et al. (2016)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016ApJ...820L..31T/abstract).

## Population Statistics and Survey Facilities

The global population of Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) is characterized by an exceptionally high all-sky [[event-rate|Event rate]]. Estimates from early single-dish searches at 1.4 GHz inferred an occurrence rate of $\sim 7 \times 10^3$ bursts sky$^{-1}$ day$^{-1}$ above a fluence of 0.6 Jy ms [Burke-Spolaor et al. (2016)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016ApJ...826..223B/abstract). Subsequent [[large-area-radio-surveys|Large area radio surveys]] have refined these constraints across different frequencies. For example, the GBNCC survey operating at 350 MHz estimates a rate of $3.4_{-3.3}^{+15.4} \times 10^3$ sky$^{-1}$ day$^{-1}$ above 0.42 Jy [Parent et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020ApJ...904...92P/abstract), while the Apertif ALERT survey at 1370 MHz measures a rate of $459_{-155}^{+208}$ sky$^{-1}$ day$^{-1}$ above a fluence limit of 4.1 Jy ms [Pastor-Marazuela et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240600482P/abstract). 

Translating the observed sky rate into a volumetric event rate density allows for direct demographic comparisons with other astrophysical transients. Assuming a Schechter function for the [[radio-luminosity-function|Radio luminosity function]], Bayesian modelling of known bursts yields a characteristic event rate density of $\sim 3.5 \times 10^4 \text{ Gpc}^{-3} \text{ yr}^{-1}$ for bursts above a luminosity of $10^{42} \text{ erg s}^{-1}$ [Luo et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.494..665L/abstract). Theoretical bounds on the local spatial density of FRB-emitting sources, constrained by the repetition statistics of known emitters, place the source density between $2.2 \times 10^2$ and $5.2 \times 10^4 \text{ Gpc}^{-3} \text{ yr}^{-1}$ [Law et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022ApJ...927...55L/abstract). 

The intrinsic [[radio-luminosity-function|Radio luminosity function]] and energy distribution of the FRB population remain areas of active study. Analyses of a well-defined sample of 63 bursts detected by the ASKAP telescope indicate that the energy distribution between $10^{23}$ and $10^{26} \text{ J Hz}^{-1}$ can be modeled as either a pure power-law with a differential slope of $\gamma = -1.96 \pm 0.15$, or a Schechter function with $\gamma = -1.82 \pm 0.12$ and an exponential cutoff energy $E_{\rm max} \sim 6.3 \times 10^{25} \text{ J Hz}^{-1}$ [Arcus et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240809351A/abstract). Furthermore, there is now $3\sigma$ evidence for [[radio-luminosity-function-evolution|luminosity evolution]] within the FRB population; the comoving density formation rate has been shown to decrease rapidly with redshift, a trend that may potentially track the rate of compact star mergers rather than strictly following the star formation history [Champati et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025ApJ...988L..64C/abstract). Fluence cumulative distributions from the Apertif survey also broadly agree with Euclidean Universe predictions, exhibiting a power-law index of $-1.23 \pm 0.06$ [Pastor-Marazuela et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240600482P/abstract). While individual repeating sources can exhibit much steeper power-law luminosity distributions—such as an index of $\alpha \approx -4.6$ for the highly active FRB 20201124A [Lanman et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022ApJ...927...59L/abstract)—it remains unclear whether the energy distributions of repeating and non-repeating FRBs are drawn from the same underlying [[radio-source-populations|physical population]].

The dramatic expansion of FRB demographics has been driven primarily by next-generation interferometric facilities. The Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment (CHIME) has revolutionized low-frequency (400-800 MHz) statistics, discovering hundreds of new bursts and isolating a robust sample of [[repeating-fast-radio-bursts|Repeating fast radio bursts]] [CHIME/FRB Collaboration et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019ApJ...885L..24C/abstract), [Pilia et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021Univ....8....9P/abstract). The sheer volume of CHIME detections has enabled large-scale statistical comparisons, revealing that repeating bursts generally exhibit significantly wider pulse durations than apparent non-repeaters, hinting at potentially divergent emission mechanisms [CHIME/FRB Collaboration et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019ApJ...885L..24C/abstract). 

Complementarily, the Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP) has been critical for probing the high-fluence regime and mapping the host galaxy population. A wide-field ASKAP survey successfully demonstrated a direct macroscopic relationship between burst dispersion measure and brightness, proving that high-fluence bursts are the local analogues of distant faint bursts [Shannon et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018Natur.562..386S/abstract). Furthermore, ASKAP's ability to localize bursts to sub-arcsecond precision from single pulses has provided the definitive host galaxy associations required to establish volumetric rates, absolute energy scales, and local environmental metrics [Bhandari et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020ApJ...895L..37B/abstract), [Bhandari et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022AJ....163...69B/abstract), [Arcus et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240809351A/abstract). In addition, the Deep Synoptic Array (DSA-110) has begun compiling a uniform host catalog of non-repeating localized FRBs. Early results from DSA-110 indicate a wide delay-time distribution for these sources, which is consistent with progenitor channels driven by binary stellar evolution [Law et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...967...29L/abstract).

## Open Questions and Future Directions

Despite rapid observational progress, the fundamental nature of fast radio bursts remains an active area of investigation. A central debate in the field revolves around the repeater vs. non-repeater dichotomy: whether all sources eventually repeat, or if there are two distinct physical populations governed by different progenitor mechanisms [Palaniswamy et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018ApJ...854L..12P/abstract), [Bhattacharya et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020ApJ...899..124B/abstract). Phenomenologically, [[repeating-fast-radio-bursts|Repeating fast radio bursts]] tend to exhibit wider pulse durations and more complex frequency-time morphologies compared to apparently non-repeating events [CHIME/FRB Collaboration et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019ApJ...885L..24C/abstract). Statistical analyses of bursts detected in the far sidelobes of the CHIME telescope suggest that either all FRBs repeat with a very wide range of intervals, or non-repeaters form a genuinely distinct population [Lin et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...975...75L/abstract). Furthermore, the detection of periodic activity windows in a small subset of repeaters—such as a 160-day cycle in FRB 121102, a 16-day cycle in FRB 180916B, and a possible 126-day cycle in FRB 20240209A—hints at binary progenitor systems or precessing magnetars, complicating efforts to establish a unified model [Pal et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025ApJ...983L..15P/abstract).

Resolving this dichotomy requires detailed studies of FRB host environments. While sub-arcsecond and milliarcsecond localization using very-long-baseline interferometry (VLBI) has associated some FRBs with [[persistent-radio-sources|Persistent radio sources]] in dwarf star-forming galaxies (e.g., FRB 121102; [Marcote et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017ApJ...834L...8M/abstract)), others have been found in massive spirals, quiescent ellipticals, or even globular clusters [Marcote et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020Natur.577..190M/abstract), [Kirsten et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022Natur.602..585K/abstract). Recent milliarcsecond localizations, such as the European VLBI Network's $\lesssim 90 \times 30$ mas precision for FRB 20240114A, have pinpointed sources to satellite dwarf galaxies, underscoring the diversity of FRB environments [Bhardwaj et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025ApJ...992L..35B/abstract). It remains an open question whether the [[compact-radio-sources|Compact radio sources]] seen co-located with some repeaters are a necessary feature of the central engine (such as a young magnetar wind nebula) or an independent phenomenon [Metzger et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017ApJ...841...14M/abstract), [Wang et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251207140W/abstract).

Future observational campaigns aim to exploit FRBs as cosmological probes by discovering them at increasingly greater distances. The recent localization of high-redshift FRBs, notably FRB 20240304B at $z=2.148$, demonstrates that these transients can trace ionized baryons across the majority of cosmic history, reaching back to the peak of cosmic star formation [Caleb et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250801648C/abstract). To fully leverage the Macquart relation (the correlation between dispersion measure and redshift) for precision cosmography, larger samples of localized bursts are required to break degeneracies between the intergalactic medium and host galaxy dispersion contributions [Wang et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023ApJ...944...50W/abstract), [Li et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025ApJ...989...77L/abstract).

Next-generation observatories, particularly the Square Kilometre Array (SKA), will revolutionize this pursuit. The SKA is projected to detect more than one FRB per minute over the entire sky, extending detections into the epoch of reionization [Fialkov et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017ApJ...846L..27F/abstract). Combined with real-time sub-arcsecond localization capabilities, these large-area [[radio-surveys|Radio surveys]] will transform FRBs into high-precision tools for mapping the cosmic web, measuring the "missing" baryons, and tracing the cosmological evolution of magnetic fields [Macquart et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015aska.confE..55M/abstract), [Cordes et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019ARA&A..57..417C/abstract).
